We’re beginning a process of publishing more frequent reports on model behavior, beyond what appears in our system cards and regular risk reports.

Today’s report describes four types of behaviors we’ve identified during evaluations and internal use. In each, Claude acted on real websites or systems in ways we didn’t intend, sometimes by working around a restriction instead of stopping. 

All cases had minimal real-world impact. From an alignment and security perspective, we consider these behaviors significantly less severe than the cybersecurity incidents we reported in July and September.

Title: Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions

Published Time: 2026-10-09T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
This report describes examples of unintended model actions we’ve observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude. It is part of our effort to publish more frequent standalone reports on model behavior and alignment beyond our system cards, which we publish with each model release, and our risk reports, which we publish every three to six months as part of our Responsible Scaling Policy. We believe it’s important to be transparent about what we see our models do during testing and use.

The behaviors can be grouped into four categories:

*   Claude exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server;
*   Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have;
*   Claude working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee; and
*   Claude using URL shortening services to get around limits in its fetch tool.

We have chosen not to name the organizations involved in the examples below to avoid exposing vulnerabilities in their systems, and at their request. For this reason, we also provide less detail about each case than we otherwise would. Some of the cases described below involved websites run by U.S. government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels. We have briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved.

The cases we’ve identified to date in these categories had minimal real-world impact. We consider these behaviors to be significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective than the cybersecurity incidents we reported on [July 30](https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals) and [September 9](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents). They resemble behaviors that we’ve described in our system cards since [Claude Mythos Preview](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/08ab9158070959f88f296514c21b7facce6f52bc.pdf). Most are forms of _persistence_, in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping.

Although the impact of these behaviors was minimal and we had already turned off live internet access for some high-risk and cybersecurity evaluations, we have now decided to expand that to include all our internal evaluations until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures (described in the remediation section of this post) reliably catch behaviors like these. Below, we also discuss alignment considerations and give more detail on how we’re modifying training to reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.

We identified most of these cases through a review of transcripts that we began in July. Our review first focused on our cybersecurity evaluations—tests where a model is deliberately asked to probe or attack a test system, and where internet access is meant to be disabled. We have since extended our scanning to encompass a much wider range of instances where Claude could have reached the internet, including tests where internet access is deliberately enabled so Claude can be evaluated on real-world tasks. We began by looking for incidents of similar severity to the cybersecurity incidents we reported this summer; we have not found any to date. We then broadened the search to lower-severity cases, where a model interacted with real websites or systems in ways we didn’t intend.

We are also now scanning a much larger pool of lower-risk transcripts, as well as our use of Claude within Anthropic and in reinforcement learning (RL) environments where Claude has access to the internet. As this work continues, we plan to report new instances of unintended behaviors. All cases reported here involved Claude interacting with the outside world; to our knowledge, none of them involved customer data or Anthropic’s own internal systems.

In this post, we explain why we run evaluations, which are where most of these cases occurred; describe each behavior in more detail; and offer a preliminary view of what the behaviors suggest about Claude’s alignment and how we’re mitigating them.

### **Why and how we run evaluations**

The behaviors described in this post are not specific to evaluations, but many of the cases we’ve identified to date occurred during evaluation runs. We continually test models on a wide range of tasks prior to releasing them. We use many different evaluations (standardized sets of tasks, scored the same way each time), each of which helps to paint a picture of Claude’s skills in a particular area. Many of the evaluations we use are public; they are written by outside researchers and can be run by any developer, allowing us to compare capabilities across models. Other evaluations we build in-house.

Because language models are non-deterministic—that is, their responses always involve some element of randomness, and they may carry out the same task slightly differently each time—we have Claude complete each evaluation task hundreds or thousands of times (each attempt is called a run). Testing so many times allows us to understand how a model typically performs, and also to catch rare cases where a model does something we don’t expect. What we learn from evaluations shapes decisions across Anthropic, including how we train models, what safeguards we build around them, and when we release them.

Evaluations are also where a model’s behavioral issues are sometimes first revealed. Models learn much of what they can do through RL, in which they attempt a task within a specific environment many times over and are rewarded when they succeed. However, training environments are imperfect. If training rewards something we didn’t intend—such as finding loopholes or working around a restriction—the model learns that the workaround pays off and may then apply it elsewhere. This is known as reward hacking. While we have processes in place to identify and filter out reward hacking during training, evaluations are a critical mechanism for understanding a model’s behavioral propensities in different contexts and on different sets of tasks than those we have in training.

Some tasks—such as searching the web for hard-to-find information—are difficult to realistically simulate in an environment without internet access. Running them with access has been standard practice within the industry: public web search benchmarks are run on the live internet by default, and running them the same way allows us to compare our models with other models. Most of the cases in this report occurred during such evaluations.

### **Overview of behaviors**

Below, we describe four categories of behavior in which Claude acted on real websites and systems in ways we did not intend, each of which involved an organization or person outside Anthropic.

#### **Exploiting a basic flaw in software to run commands on a server**

When Claude could not complete an evaluation task directly, either because its own tools were deliberately limited or because an outside service it needed was unavailable, it used other tools hosted on a third party’s site to achieve its goal. In some circumstances, it did this by exploiting basic flaws in that site’s software, using SQL or command injection (a way of sending input that the site mistakenly runs as instructions).

For example, one evaluation asked Claude Mythos Preview to run a scientific analysis. The public tool it needed to perform that analysis was hosted by a university; when the model sought to access it, the tool returned an error. Looking for another way to complete the task, Claude explored the tool’s website, found a script on the university’s server that would return any file it was asked for, and used it to copy files from the server, including the script’s own code. In that code Claude found the injection flaw that let it run commands on the server, and used it to run the calculation.

In another instance, the data Claude Mythos 5 needed was free, but Claude could not access it without accepting a data use agreement, which it did not have the tools to do. Claude used applications hosted on the website to load the page and accept the agreement on its behalf.

We saw this behavior on DeepSearchQA and BrowseComp (both public web research evaluations), on LABBench2 (a public biology research benchmark), and during internal evaluations.

#### **Submitting a form it should not have**

We saw instances where Claude submitted an online form when it shouldn’t have. Generally, this occurred when an evaluation’s instructions were ambiguous, or when a misconfiguration within the environment prevented Claude from working with dummy forms.

For example, in a case that happened multiple times on the same evaluation, an unreleased, non-frontier research model was meant to fill out a practice copy of a government form. When the copy failed to load or the model closed it by mistake, the model instead navigated to the website where the real form is normally hosted and submitted the form there.

In another evaluation, Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete a form up until the final submission stage, but to stop before actually submitting. Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page. In these instances, the model’s chain-of-thought stated that it was demonstrating the process, not submitting a real request.

In a third example of this behavior, Claude Haiku 4.5 had been tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages. In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the following: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” (The website did not include a description of the perpetrator.) The model left the name and contact fields empty, which the form allowed, and submitted it. The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation.

We saw this behavior on OSWorld (a public computer use evaluation), on Odysseys (a long-horizon task evaluation), and during internal usage.

#### **Working around restrictions to reach gated data**

Claude sometimes worked around a restriction to reach data to which it did not have access. Generally, this occurred when a server refused Claude’s request, or when the data was offered only for a fee.

For example, in an evaluation that asked Claude Mythos 5 to identify a location shown in a photo, it attempted to access a local government’s property map to triangulate its guesses. Claude could read webpage text, but the evaluation limited its ability to click through it as a person would. Instead, it read the settings file the site sends to browsers, found working access tokens, and used them to send requests directly to the server behind the map to access the data.

In another example of this behavior, an Anthropic researcher used Claude Mythos 5 on a statistics project that required it to pull public data that was available from a state agency for a fee. Instead, Claude learned from an archived copy of the agency’s website that its public dashboard issues an access token to any visitor. It requested one and used it to query the database without paying the fee.

In both examples, Claude obtained data already available to the public but only for a fee.

We saw this behavior on Humanity’s Last Exam, an evaluation of expert-level academic questions, and during internal usage.

#### **Using URL shortening services**

Some of our fetch tools, which let Claude read webpages, limit the length of the URLs Claude can request. This limit is in place to reduce the risk from Claude using long URLs to take certain unwanted actions, such as exfiltrating larger amounts of data. We saw several models, including Claude Opus 5 and Claude Mythos 5, get around this limitation by using free URL shortening services. We first identified this behavior internally, but as we were writing this post, an operator of the da.gd URL shortening service let us know that they had also found Claude using their website for this purpose. We thank the operator for sharing these details.

### **Remediation**

We’ve taken several preventive measures. Some of the public evaluations we no longer run; others we have moved to their offline versions, or rebuilt them so that their tasks do not reach live websites. We’ve also made broader changes. We have updated the guardrails on some of our internet access tools, such as the web fetch tool, to heavily restrict what the model can do with them. And, as part of our ongoing [agent security and monitoring efforts](https://www.anthropic.com/news/improving-alignment-security-efforts), we have built tooling to automatically detect and block the kinds of behaviors described above. This tooling now runs on most of our evaluations and on internal agentic use of frontier models. When we tested it against the cases described in this post, it blocked all of them.

As we described in our August 31 [post](https://www.anthropic.com/news/improving-alignment-security-efforts), we are also continuing to fix or remove training environments that reward Claude for working around tool restrictions or other blockers, so that they do not incentivize these behaviors or permit reward hacking.

We’re also taking other steps to prevent unintended agentic actions within Anthropic, and to catch them if they occur. These include migrating internal agents to centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment, minimizing internet access for internal agents and training processes, and monitoring far more of what agents do through techniques like [safety classifiers](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/cheap-monitors/) and [hierarchical summarization](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2025/summarization-for-monitoring/). These measures are now part of our security team’s detection and response procedures so that we can respond to and contain undesired behavior quickly. We expect to publish more on these approaches, and to build them directly into our products.

### **Discussion and alignment takeaways**

While we have not completed a full alignment assessment of these cases, we consider them to be less severe than the cybersecurity incidents from this summer. We explain why below, and share the general lessons we’ve drawn from them.

#### **Alignment context**

As we establish a regular public reporting process for behaviors like these, we also want to situate them in terms of their severity. This remains challenging: judging the extent of an alignment failure often depends on what the model was trying to do, and a model’s own account of its reasoning is not necessarily reliable evidence of its beliefs or reasons for action, as we discussed in our September 9 [alignment assessment](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents). As models grow more capable, they can interact with the world in more sophisticated ways, which makes more complex failures possible. For example, the biased reasoning we described in that assessment was not new, but it led to more serious consequences in a setting where models could capably act on real systems for hours at a time. An alignment severity framework built around today’s failures could become outdated quickly, given how fast AI capabilities are advancing.

Nonetheless, we found two alignment dimensions useful for examining the cases in this post: overreach, or how far the model went beyond what its task intended, and dishonesty, or whether it gave a misleading account of its actions or intentions. On overreach, we consider these cases to be substantially less concerning than the incidents we reported this summer, in which Claude gained access to real third-party systems for hours during cybersecurity evaluations. In the cases we report here, in contrast, Claude bypassed access controls to reach gated but publicly available data, or exploited software flaws and ran commands on servers (mainly to reach non-sensitive data).

On dishonesty, the comparison is more mixed. In one case, tasked with generating example interactions with websites, Claude submitted an invented tip through a police department’s online form. From the transcript, Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal. In the most serious [incident from this summer,](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents) by contrast, Claude’s misleading reasoning was sustained over hours and supported its continued attack. Still, judging dishonesty with confidence typically requires a deeper assessment than we have done here, such as replaying transcripts with modifications to test what drove the model’s behavior, so our view of these cases may change with further analysis.

#### **Lessons and next steps**

None of the behaviors we’ve described here are new, and they do not change our overall view of Claude’s alignment. In many of the cases where we observed these behaviors, Claude had been given tasks that were ambiguous or impossible to complete. We and others have observed that when models are given impossible-to-complete tasks, they will pursue unintended and sometimes misaligned strategies to achieve their goals.

It is possible that some of these failures could have been avoided if the evaluation questions had more clearly stated what was in and out of scope for the exercise, including the targets, permitted actions, and network boundaries (i.e., what the model should and shouldn’t access). However, Claude encounters ambiguous and impossible tasks every day in real use, and, indeed, several of the cases we observed occurred during regular agentic use of Claude.

Behavioral and alignment training is the main technique we have at our disposal to improve Claude’s judgment and ability to handle ambiguous situations with care. Historically, we have been more focused on teaching models to respect boundaries and be appropriately cautious in coding environments. We are now expanding these environments to applications like search and computer use, which were involved in the cases described here. However, alignment training is not yet sufficient or fully robust on its own, at least in the short term, so we also rely on defense-in-depth approaches, including the classifiers and safeguards described above.

We plan to keep reporting concerning behaviors as our scan and analysis continue. We hope these reports help other developers check for similar behaviors in their own models, since many of the evaluations involved are public and widely used. While these cases had minimal impact, we do not want to diminish the findings, because the same behaviors could do far more harm as models become more powerful. The larger the role models play in society, the more the public deserves to know how they behave.

_Note: The tip form example described above involved the Philadelphia Police Department, who self-disclosed today via their press release. We shared this finding with the department on October 8 as soon as our technical review was complete._

_Corrected Oct 12, 2026:_ A previous version of this post incorrectly stated that Claude's web fetch limits were put in place to prevent SQL or command injections. In a small number of evaluation runs

article.description:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

quoted_tweet.author: karpathy
quoted_tweet.text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

Today @TheLancet published our AMIE study with @BIDMC_Medicine, the first prospective study of patient-facing conversational diagnostics in a real clinic.

AMIE is a research system people can chat with before doctors appointments. Testing AMIE outside the lab with real urgent care patients showed how technology can help gather medical histories safely. Clinicians reported that the summaries helped them prepare for visits in 75% of cases and influenced their approach to care in more than half. AMIE’s differential diagnoses also matched the doctors’ final diagnoses 90% of the time giving clinicians more time to focus on patient care.

It’s Google’s first-ever paper in The Lancet’s main journal!

article.description:
Introducing QwenGyre, bringing elastic RL to extreme-long-horizon (XLong) agent training. ✨

It launches with two core designs: 🥳
- Elastic Scheduler: reallocates GPUs between rollout & training as demand shifts—live executions never interrupted. Up to 1.85× speedup over Colocate, 1.78× over Async.
- Trajectory Processor: turns branching executions (compaction, sub-agents, retries) into prefix-shared trajectory trees with bounded, deduplicated training samples. Partial progress after timeout still gets scored.

Scaled to Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B with ~700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre lifts NL2RepoBench from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps, cutting end-to-end training time by ~44% vs Async.

We’re exploring how AI can accelerate health science research.

While AI has made significant breakthroughs in formal sciences like mathematics, health data science depends on imperfect real-world data and consequential choices about cohorts, variables, and causal assumptions.

To explore how AI can assist health researchers, we built a human-led research scaffold powered by Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder with access to 5M retrospective de-identified electronic health records and publicly available data. A cohort of medical experts used the system to conduct original research, accelerate hypothesis generation, code execution, and manuscript drafting while maintaining full authority over scientific decisions.

Today, we’re sharing 10 research manuscripts produced through this exploration, spanning cardiology, oncology, infectious disease, emergency medicine, and more.

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. article.description:
Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

3. Similarly, we first had Mythos-class models in February but didn’t make them generally available until June (when we had stronger cyber safeguards in place). We only offered them to a limited set of partners in order to focus on cyberdefense. It would have been much more economically rational to simply release the model to everyone. We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead. But because of this, many companies secured their cyber infrastructure before the deluge of widely available cyber-capable models. Of course there are ways it could have gone better or been run better, but this was what we were aiming to do.

4. I advocated forcefully and publicly, in my essay Policy on the AI Exponential in June of this year, for the government to have the power to block model releases. Back then this was still outside or maybe on the edge of the Overton window, though I understand the window has moved since then. We were attacked intensely for this.

5. I don’t want to re-ignite conflict, but the events of February 2026 are a strong example. It is clear that our public stance could have seriously damaged the company’s future.

6. We’ve continued to advocate for export controls on chips and chipmaking equipment to China, because we think it allows democracies to negotiate from a position of strength on AI safety agreements. We’ve done this despite problems it’s created for us with industry partners who hold very different views and on whom we are very dependent.

7. As far as I’m aware we were the first, and still only, frontier company to restrict the sale of AI services to PRC-controlled companies, including those operating through third countries (otherwise a major loophole). We’ve therefore forfeited significant short-term business to prevent fueling AI platforms and applications that would help the CCP’s military and intelligence services. We are also cracking down on distillation; generally, distillation is not a major threat to us commercially, but like chip exports it has concerning national security and safety implications, so we expend significant energy and company resources to address it.

8. As you mentioned, we’ve put out a lot of reports, announcements, long model cards, public advocacy, etc, all trying to inform the public about the risks of AI. These involve a level of detail and effort that would be implausible for a purely profit-maximizing company.

9. Just this week, we announced we were putting 5% (and possibly more over time) of the company into a public benefit fund.

All of these decisions came with very substantial costs to us. To be fair, those that involved holding back or restricting access to frontier capabilities also had a broader cost — for example, the public might otherwise have benefitted from faster progress in biology, so I am not saying that our decisions were without tradeoffs — but they were not driven by profit-seeking.

For each decision, you can come up with ulterior motives that could have driven us — I think it is a general truth that any decision, on any topic, can always be portrayed as a nefarious scheme. But most of those end up being pretty farfetched or don’t fully make sense if you actually examine them closely. For example, it is deeply implausible that it would be a shrewd business move to block a large swath of research biology in order to do the work ourselves and compete with our customers; we expect the benefit to the ecosystem to greatly exceed the work Anthropic does itself, and for the two to complement each other. It is not in Anthropic’s interest to be perceived as unfriendly to biologists. Our Life Sciences Verification Program, which gives vetted biology professionals access to our models, also refutes this idea. 

Of course, a different set of people will see this and make a different criticism: that Anthropic shouldn't be making decisions about who gets access to what in the first place. I agree, in the sense that ideally the government would be making these decisions, and that’s why we advocate for regulation. But for now we are forced to make them, and enabling bioterrorism isn’t a better option.

I think that even if I conceded every item in your list, I would happily hold up mine next to it; I don’t think it’s a close call. That is of course partly subjective and different things are important to different people. Maybe one way you could object is that several of the items above relate to AI misuse and not loss-of-control; if you think the latter is much more important than the former, that might change your calculus. But this is not Anthropic’s view — we view both as serious issues. You can also disagree with our decisions, as many have, but they are consistent.

But I also disagree with at least some of your list. Several items don’t represent a deviation from Anthropic’s strategy or values at all, once we postulate the “race to the top” strategy that requires being a frontier AI company. Your items 1-4 are all simply examples of what it means to compete at the frontier, and we stand by them, both in the sense that they are transparently ordinary things to do as part of that strategy, and that we stand by the strategy as a whole. 

To be fair, there are important questions worth confronting (and that we are confronting) about what to do when the AI-driven acceleration gets fast enough that it is hard for safety to keep up. We are nearing that point and that’s what’s driving some of our thinking about “pacing.” But 1-4 are actions taken before that point and should be perfectly expected based on Anthropic’s strategy as a company. Of course it is possible to disagree with that strategy, but that’s a more fundamental disagreement that you could have had any time over the last few years.

I agree we could have handled your items 7, 8, and 9 better. All fall into the category of “rhetoric or policy communication that wasn’t carefully written or resulting from fast-changing circumstances not propagating from one team to another fast enough.” This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations (Anthropic is over 5,000 people), and doesn’t even necessarily represent a failure or mistake of any single person. I am of course the CEO, and I take responsibility. The volume of communication from Anthropic is enormous and if these are the worst examples, I think we’re frankly doing pretty well, though I will continue to work hard to make sure we do even better.

Your 5th item (the change to our RSP) is the most substantive item, and people can debate this, but I think that the old, more rigid RSP created a lot of situations where we were technically required to do something that required a lot of effort but in retrospect wasn’t very important for safety, as well as not covering some of the most important things. Our current RSP’s focus on transparency brought things like risk reports and roadmaps, and its emphasis on independent external review laid the groundwork for even more intensive embedded evaluation, all of which I think have been valuable in driving a race to the top. In the original announcement in September 2023, we described the RSP as an “early iteration that we [would] build on” and said that “rapid iteration…will almost certainly be necessary.” I understand that changing plans is always a move that creates justifiable scrutiny — I just don’t think we ever represented that we wouldn’t do so.

Relating to your 6th item (having an FCF in addition to our RSP), I know our intent is to meet the letter and spirit of our regulatory obligations (via our FCF) while also remaining able to experiment with more novel approaches to risk management that go beyond what the law currently requires (via our RSP). I promise to look into it further, as it’s a complex issue and it is possible we are not weighing the considerations in the right way.

Overall, although Anthropic has made plenty of mistakes as an organization — including some of the items on your list — I feel that we have repeatedly taken serious and substantive actions counter to our bottom line and that there is a significant negativity bias distorting assessments like the one you are making above. We’ll always try to do better but, again, I am extremely proud of our track record and stand by it. I will have more to say soon about how we are going to further live our values in this moment of rapid change.

quoted_tweet.text:
Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies  will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

 “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: 

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet…  incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. 

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. But I have every confidence that if employees at Anthropic saw one of their competitors (e.g. at OpenAI) take some of these actions, they would take it as confirmation of all their worst suspicions. (They might even call OpenAI employees a little gullible for accepting their leadership’s explanations for this behavior at face value.) 

Perhaps these were mistakes in the sense that they are not decisions that Anthropic leadership would endorse, but the actions still happened because of incentives and decisions that Anthropic leadership is ultimately responsible for (and would not accept similar excuses from another organization).

When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests? For every provision that was too weak or a giveaway to AI companies in this legislation, why wasn’t there a mistake pushing in the direction of being too strong?

A core part of Anthropic’s theory of change is that being at the frontier gives you more leverage to advocate for stricter policy. I think that conceptually makes sense, but in practice I’ve seen Anthropic push the frontier without substantially pushing the ‘safety frontier’ a remotely equivalent amount.

I want to end by quoting from Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah’s comments around the Magnifica Humanitas release:

“Every frontier AI lab—including Anthropic—operates inside a set of incentives and constraints that can sometimes conflict with doing the right thing. The pressure to stay commercially viable and to stay at the research frontier. Geopolitical pressure. And the older, plainer pressures of pride and ambition. No matter how sincerely any of us intend to do the right thing—and I believe many of us do—we will always be influenced by those incentives.

That is why, if we want this technology to go well, it is enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

I hope these remarks are taken in that constructive spirit, and not as an attack on anyone specific at the organization (certainly not you Anthony, who I have only personally seen act professionally and thoughtfully, and who only ended up getting this diatribe in your replies for random contingent reasons).
